arch.title: Batch or streaming?
arch.subtitle: Two ways to feed a data lake, running side by side. A batch ETL where a cron job full-loads the source table into the raw layer on a schedule, and streaming, where Kafka and Flink clean events in real time, in parallel, straight into the silver layer.
arch.goal1: Send a few events and follow them end to end.
arch.goal2: In batch ETL, watch how long new data waits for the next cron run.
arch.goal3: Take Flink down, keep sending, bring it back, then hit replay.
arch.goal4: Compare the data lake cost: a full load re-copies everything, every run.
arch.diagramLabelKafka: Animated diagram: producers send events through Kafka to Apache Flink, which processes them in parallel and writes them to the silver layer of the data lake.
arch.diagramLabelBatch: Animated diagram: producers write to a source database, and a cron job periodically copies the whole table into the raw layer of the data lake.

caption.kafkaIdle: Each event lands in the Kafka log, and Flink reads both partitions in parallel, cleaning and enriching events on the fly. They reach the silver layer already usable, about a second after they happen.
caption.kafkaBuffering: Spike absorbed: Kafka is holding {{count}} events while Flink works at its own pace. Nothing is lost, it just catches up.
caption.kafkaDown: Flink is down, but events keep landing safely in Kafka ({{count}} waiting). When it comes back, it resumes from its last committed offset, the blue marker.
caption.kafkaReplay: Replay: Flink rewound to the oldest retained offset and is reprocessing history into the silver layer. Same data, new pipeline logic, nothing re-sent.
caption.batchIdle: Batch ETL: producers write to a source database, and a cron job copies the whole table into the raw layer on a schedule. Between runs, nothing reaches the lake.
caption.batchWaiting: {{count}} new events are sitting in the source database. They only reach the data lake on the next cron run, in {{seconds}}s, and they land raw, still needing another job to clean them.
caption.batchLoading: Full load running: copying all {{count}} rows, including every row already loaded in previous runs. The bigger the table, the slower and pricier each run gets.
caption.kafkaDown_one: Flink is down, but events keep landing safely in Kafka (1 waiting). When it comes back, it resumes from its last committed offset, the blue marker.
caption.batchWaiting_one: 1 new event is sitting in the source database. It only reaches the data lake on the next cron run, in {{seconds}}s, and it lands raw, still needing another job to clean it.
caption.batchLoading_one: Full load running: copying the 1 row in the table. Every future run will copy everything again, including this one.

gateway.title: One door, with a shield
gateway.subtitle: Kong Gateway sits in front of every service. It authenticates, rate limits and routes each request, so the services behind it only ever see clean, expected traffic.
gateway.goal1: Send a few requests and watch Kong route them.
gateway.goal2: Launch a bot flood with and without the gateway.
gateway.goal3: Send a request without a token in both modes.
gateway.goal4: Compare how many real users end up with errors.
gateway.diagramKong: Animated diagram: clients send requests through Kong Gateway, which blocks unauthenticated and excessive traffic and routes the rest to three services.
gateway.diagramDirect: Animated diagram: clients send requests straight to three services with no gateway in front of them.

caption.kongIdle: Every request passes through Kong first. It checks the token, enforces rate limits and routes to the right service, so the services only see clean traffic.
caption.kongBlocking: The shield is up: Kong rejected {{count}} requests (429 too many requests, 401 unauthorized) before they could touch a service.
caption.directIdle: No gateway: every service is exposed and has to implement auth, rate limiting and routing by itself, each one slightly differently.
caption.directOverload: The flood hit the services directly. They are overloaded, and real users get errors too: {{count}} failed requests so far.
caption.directExposed: A request without a token went straight to a service. Unless every team implemented auth perfectly, that is a hole.
caption.directOverload_one: The flood hit the services directly. They are overloaded, and real users get errors too: 1 failed request so far.

auth.title: Log in once, everywhere
auth.subtitle: Keycloak speaks OpenID Connect: apps hand authentication to one identity provider and get signed tokens back, which any API can verify on its own.
auth.goal1: Log in to the portal, then open the dashboard.
auth.goal2: Compare how many passwords you type in each mode.
auth.goal3: Call the API and see who validates the request.
auth.goal4: With SSO, expire the token, call the API again, then log out.
auth.diagramSso: Animated diagram: two apps delegate login to Keycloak over OpenID Connect and call an API with signed tokens.
auth.diagramLocal: Animated diagram: two apps each keep their own user table and login, and the API calls an app back to validate sessions.

caption.needLogin: Log in to the portal first.
caption.ssoIdle: With Keycloak, apps never see passwords. They redirect to one identity provider, get signed OpenID Connect tokens back, and any API can verify those tokens on its own.
caption.ssoLogin: The portal redirected you to Keycloak. You typed your password once, and Keycloak sent back a signed ID token and access token.
caption.ssoSecondApp: Single sign-on: the dashboard asked Keycloak too, which already knew you. You are in, without typing a password again.
caption.ssoApi: The API checked the token's signature with Keycloak's cached public keys. No round trip, no shared session database.
caption.ssoRefresh: The access token had expired, so the API answered 401. The app used its refresh token with Keycloak and retried, without asking you anything.
caption.ssoExpired: Access tokens are short-lived on purpose. Call the API now and see what happens.
caption.ssoLogout: Single logout: one click ended the Keycloak session, and every app logged you out together.
caption.localIdle: Without an identity provider, every app keeps its own user table and its own login screen. More passwords, and more places to leak them.
caption.localLogin: The portal checked your password against its own user table.
caption.localSecondApp: The dashboard has a separate user table, so you had to log in again, with another password to remember.
caption.localApi: The API cannot trust the portal's session on its own, so it called the portal back to validate it. Every request pays that round trip.
caption.localLogout: You logged out of the portal, but the dashboard still has its own session open. Logging out is not really logging out.

k8s.title: Same app, cloud and on-premise
k8s.subtitle: Kubernetes runs the same manifests on a cloud cluster and an on-premise cluster. It scales with traffic, heals itself when a machine dies and ships new versions without downtime.
k8s.goal1: Fire a traffic spike in both modes and watch the replicas.
k8s.goal2: Kill a node and see who fixes it.
k8s.goal3: Deploy v2 and count the failed requests.
k8s.goal4: Notice the same deployment runs in the cloud and on-premise.
k8s.diagramK8s: Animated diagram: an ingress routes traffic to pods spread over a cloud cluster and an on-premise cluster managed by Kubernetes.
k8s.diagramServers: Animated diagram: a load balancer routes traffic to six hand-managed servers, three in the cloud and three on-premise.

caption.k8sIdle: Same manifests, two clusters: Kubernetes runs the app in the cloud and on-premise the same way, and keeps the number of replicas you declared.
caption.k8sSpike: Traffic spike: the autoscaler saw the load and is running {{count}} pods across both clusters. When the spike ends, it scales back down.
caption.k8sNode: A node died. Kubernetes noticed and rescheduled its pods on healthy nodes, in the cloud or on-premise, without anyone being paged.
caption.k8sDeploy: Rolling update: each v2 pod must be ready before a v1 pod is removed, so users never see downtime.
caption.serversIdle: Hand-managed servers: one app per machine, sized for the worst day and configured by hand in each environment.
caption.serversSpike: Spike: six fixed servers cannot grow. {{count}} requests have failed so far.
caption.serversNode: A server died and the load balancer keeps sending it traffic. Someone has to wake up and fix it by hand.
caption.serversDeploy: Manual deploy: each server goes down while it is updated, one at a time. Requests that hit it fail, and cloud and on-premise can drift apart.
caption.serversSpike_one: Spike: six fixed servers cannot grow. 1 request has failed so far.

obs.title: See problems before users do
obs.subtitle: Services emit metrics, logs and traces through OpenTelemetry, and Grafana turns them into live dashboards and alerts. The difference shows up in one number: how long it takes to notice.
obs.goal1: Inject slowness in payments and see how fast each mode notices.
obs.goal2: Inject errors and compare the time to detect.
obs.goal3: With Grafana, follow the alert to the service at fault.
obs.goal4: Fix the incident and watch the dashboard recover.
obs.panelTitle: checkout · p95 latency and error rate
obs.diagramGrafana: Animated diagram: requests flow through gateway, orders and payments while OpenTelemetry feeds a live Grafana dashboard.
obs.diagramBlind: Animated diagram: requests flow through gateway, orders and payments with no telemetry collected.

caption.grafanaIdle: Every service ships metrics, logs and traces through OpenTelemetry to Grafana. You see the system's real behavior, live, before anyone complains.
caption.grafanaIncident: Something just went wrong. Watch the dashboard: the line is climbing toward the alert threshold.
caption.grafanaDetected: Alert fired {{seconds}}s after the incident, and the trace points straight at payments. Fix it before most users notice.
caption.blindIdle: No telemetry: services run as black boxes. Things look fine, because nothing tells you otherwise.
caption.blindIncident: An incident is happening right now, and nothing on screen shows it. Requests are slow or failing, but you have no signal.
caption.blindDetected: You found out {{seconds}}s later, from a user complaint. And you still don't know which service is the problem.

ddd.title: Boundaries that match the business
ddd.subtitle: Domain-driven design splits a system into bounded contexts, each with its own model and language, talking through domain events instead of shared tables.
ddd.goal1: Place a few orders and follow the domain events.
ddd.goal2: Change the pricing rule in both modes and count what gets redeployed.
ddd.goal3: Take Billing down and keep placing orders.
ddd.goal4: Compare how many orders fail in the monolith.
ddd.diagramDdd: Animated diagram: four bounded contexts, Orders, Catalog, Billing and Shipping, exchange domain events through an event bus.
ddd.diagramMonolith: Animated diagram: a monolith where four modules share one model and database and call each other synchronously.

caption.dddIdle: Each bounded context owns its model and its language: an Order in Orders is not an Invoice in Billing. They talk through domain events, not shared tables.
caption.dddOrder: Orders accepted the order and published OrderPlaced. Billing and Shipping react on their own time.
caption.dddRule: The pricing rule lives in Billing, so only Billing is redeployed. Orders, Catalog and Shipping never noticed.
caption.dddBillingDown: Billing is down, but orders keep flowing. {{count}} events are waiting on the bus and will be invoiced when Billing comes back.
caption.monoIdle: One codebase, one shared model, one database. Every module reaches into every other one, so nothing changes in isolation.
caption.monoOrder: The order went through Orders, Billing and Shipping in one synchronous call. It works, as long as every module is healthy.
caption.monoRule: Changing one pricing rule touched the shared model, so all four modules were rebuilt and the whole app redeployed. Orders fail while it restarts.
caption.monoBillingDown: Billing failed and took the order flow down with it: {{count}} orders lost.
caption.dddBillingDown_one: Billing is down, but orders keep flowing. 1 event is waiting on the bus and will be invoiced when Billing comes back.
caption.monoBillingDown_one: Billing failed and took the order flow down with it: 1 order lost.

agents.title: More hands, same judgment
agents.subtitle: I split work into well-scoped tasks and hand them to Claude Code agents, each in its own git worktree. They implement in parallel; I stay on design and review every change before it ships.
agents.goal1: Add a batch of tasks and work through them solo.
agents.goal2: Switch to agents and add the same batch.
agents.goal3: Compare how long each task takes from backlog to main.
agents.goal4: Notice where the human still matters: the review step.
agents.diagramAgents: Animated diagram: tasks flow from a backlog to three Claude Code agents working in parallel, then to a human review, then to main.
agents.diagramSolo: Animated diagram: tasks flow from a backlog to one developer who implements them one at a time, then to main.

caption.soloIdle: Working alone, tasks go one at a time: write, test, fix, repeat. The backlog moves only as fast as one person can type.
caption.soloBusy: {{count}} tasks waiting. Each one has to wait for the previous one to finish.
caption.agentsIdle: Tasks go to Claude Code agents, each in its own git worktree, so they never step on each other. I stay on design and review.
caption.agentsBusy: {{count}} agents working in parallel. Each change comes back as a PR that I review before it reaches main.
caption.agentsReview: Now the bottleneck is review, which is exactly where a human should be: the agents type, I decide what ships.
caption.agentsBusy_one: 1 agent working. Each change comes back as a PR that I review before it reaches main.

streaming.title: Event streaming platform
streaming.summary: An internal, on-premise streaming platform that lets any team publish and consume events without custom point-to-point integrations.
streaming.context: Enterprise integrations needed to move toward an event-driven model that scales and that teams can adopt on their own.
streaming.role: Technical lead within Systems Architecture, leading the platform's architecture and implementation.
decisions: Multi-broker environment: Kafka for streaming, RabbitMQ for messaging
Automated provisioning of connectors for databases and external systems into the central event bus
Apache Flink for real-time processing, transformation and enrichment
Hybrid architecture (on-premise and cloud) with cross-cluster replication
A low-code layer that hides event-driven complexity from product teams
outcomes: Integrations across the organization become decoupled and self-service
Streaming analytics and data enrichment in real time
Event-driven integration open to teams without streaming expertise

devsuite.title: Developers Suite
devsuite.summary: An internal developer platform for API and system governance, used across an ecosystem of ~900 developers.
devsuite.context: With ~900 developers building integrations, teams duplicated work and had a hard time finding which systems and APIs already existed.
devsuite.role: Software architecture researcher in the Systems Architecture and Data Governance team. Designed the platform.
decisions: A single, centralized platform for API and system governance
Standardized integration patterns shared by every team
Discoverability as a first-class feature: find systems before building new ones
outcomes: Consistent integration patterns across the ecosystem
Systems and APIs that are easy to discover

provisioning.title: Self-service infrastructure
provisioning.summary: A platform that provisions databases and Kubernetes environments on demand, without tickets.
provisioning.context: Provisioning databases and environments by hand was slow and added operational overhead for every new project.
provisioning.role: Built the provisioning platform and the CI/CD pipelines behind it.
decisions: Automated, self-service provisioning of databases and Kubernetes environments
Support for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, MinIO and Redis
Reproducible CI/CD pipelines for infrastructure and applications
Automated Kubernetes deployments focused on reliability and consistency

gateway.title: API gateway, identity and observability
gateway.summary: A shared front door for enterprise APIs, with standardized authentication and end-to-end visibility.
gateway.context: Each system reimplemented its own integration, security and monitoring logic.
gateway.role: Architected the API gateway platform and standardized auth and observability.
decisions: A centralized API gateway with Kong on Kubernetes
Evolved into a micro-gateway architecture, on-premise and in the cloud
Standardized authentication with OpenID Connect and Keycloak, including system-to-system
OpenTelemetry with centralized logs, metrics and tracing in Grafana
outcomes: Less integration logic duplicated across systems

oxid.context: My bachelor's thesis, built to explore what a gateway designed for performance from day one looks like.
oxid.role: Designed and developed it end to end.
decisions: Rust for predictable performance and memory safety
outcomes: A gateway focused on scalability, performance and production-grade reliability
Research that feeds back into how I design platforms
